newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Jewish leaders slam Papon over TV interview.
newsitem.headline: French Jewish leaders slam Papon over TV interview.

text.p: French Jewish leaders lambasted accused Nazi collaborator Maurice Papon on Wednesday for "scandalous" allegations the ex-cabinet minister made on television on the role Jews played in drawing up lists for death camp deportations.

The CRIF umbrella body for Jewish associations also hit out at private television network TF1 for a "travesty of justice" in screening the rare interview with Papon, whom the Supreme Court last week ordered to stand trial on charges of crimes against humanity.

Accused of sending 1,560 Jews, including many children, on their way to Nazi death camps, Papon, 86, said in the interview shown late on Tuesday he would tell his trial that Jews drew up lists of fellow Jews for the gas chambers.

"If it is the trial of Vichy, then the full trial must take place and there will be no avoiding the role of the General Union of French Jews, UGIF, who were auxiliaries...and took part -- under threat of course -- in these operations.

"I know a leader of CRIF, or of a similar group, whose role at Drancy (a holding camp in France) was to select those Jews who stayed in Drancy and those who were to be deported to Germany," said Papon, fiercely combative despite his age. "They did the selecting, I didn't."

In 1942-44, Papon was secretary-general of the Bordeaux prefect's office under the collaborationist Vichy government. His trial, after a 15-year legal marathon, will probably be France's last chance to put Nazi collaboration in the dock.

"The CRIF strongly expresses its total reprobation after the scandalous statements made by Maurice Papon...Papon used all manoeuvres imaginable to flee his own responsibilities, shamefully showing no hesitation in calling into question the Jewish victims of (Vichy leader) Philippe Petain," the group said in a statement.
"The CRIF seriously deplores that TF1 complacently gave a platform to a man accused of complicity in crimes against humanity in a broadcast which was a true travesty of justice," it said.
Whatever the journalist's competence, he could not act like a public prosecutor in a television studio when the rights of the defence were not respected, the statement said.
Asked about Papon's allegations, Nazi hunter Arno Klarsfeld told Reuters: "It was a question of life or death. It wasn't the Jews who arrested Jews, or who organised the round-ups."
Lawyer Gerard Boulanger, another lawyer for deportees' relatives, said a cynical Papon "took a revisionist stance to rebuild his past based on a fictitious resistance".
French Jews are still divided about UGIF, the body ordered created by the Nazis as a replica of the "Jewish Councils" formed in occupied East European countries.
UGIF was presided over by respected community leaders, and its defenders recall that its first two presidents and many other officials went to the gas chambers with their families.

They say UGIF fed tens of thousands of Jews made penniless by Nazi seizures of bank accounts and property and saved thousands of children by placing them with non-Jewish families who hid them through the war.
But critics say UGIF helped the Germans by its very existence and recall, as Papon did, that deportation lists at Drancy were indeed sometimes left to senior inmates to draw up.
Papon's acrimonious interview was recorded earlier in the day and aired in a live programme, with Klarsfeld present. Papon's attorneys ordered him not to attend for fear of assassination.
Journalist Paul Amar sought to have him look at photos of two sisters, aged five and two, he is accused of ordering brought back from a hiding place to be handed to the Germans.

"Monsieur Amar, what you are doing is showing off for your viewers," Papon said, pushing the photos aside and saying he brought the girls back because their arrested parents asked to be reunited with them whatever lay ahead.
